title: Welcome Back. LinkedIn Missed You... Not.
author: Is It Working?!
summary: The Is It Working?! newsletter delivers a satirical taxonomy of LinkedIn's worst performative genres, the vulnerability trap (crying-in-a-car-park "authenticity"), the humblebrag, the one-line-per-paragraph poet, the manufactured coffee-shop leadership lesson, and the engagement-bait open question, before pivoting to a genuinely practical argument about professional communication. Its core diagnosis is that these patterns aren't individual character flaws but an emergent effect of an algorithm that rewards performance over substance, meaning "nobody sat down and decided to become a person who posts photos of themselves at airports; it happened incrementally." Rather than dismissing the platform entirely, the piece closes with nine concrete practices for using LinkedIn as an actual professional communication tool, posting rarely but with real opinions, writing in a voice you'd use aloud, networking through direct genuine outreach rather than public posturing, and building your profile as a document rather than a monument. The underlying leadership point is that the audience whose opinion actually carries professional consequence is small and unimpressed by likes, so writing for that handful of people rather than the algorithm is the only version of LinkedIn use worth the time.
points: The piece's sharpest structural insight is that these performative genres are not individual failures of taste but an emergent property of algorithmic incentive: 'the algorithm rewards it and the engagement confirms it, so the pattern repeats again and again,' meaning even people who find it annoying end up reproducing it.

Its glossary of 'LinkedIn dialect' (learnings, unpacking, leaning into, the space, journey, pivot, thought leader) functions as a practical detector for hollow corporate language, useful for any professional auditing their own writing, not just LinkedIn posts specifically.

The distinguishing test for a genuine opinion versus empty engagement bait is concrete and reusable: 'Great panel today, so much to think about is not an opinion... I disagreed with almost everything said in the third session, and here's why is an opinion.'

The closing reframe of a professional profile as 'a document, not a monument,' meant to be read and useful rather than admired, gives leaders a concrete standard for their own self-presentation that cuts against the platform's dominant incentive toward performance.
quotes: The telltale phrase is I don't usually share things like this. Erm. The problem is that you always share things like this.
No one is writing a post because they're genuinely curious what a network of 4,000 people they've never met thinks. They're writing it because the algorithm rewards comments.
Nobody sat down and decided to become a person who posts photos of themselves at airports; it happened incrementally.
Post less but mean it more: Three posts a month that say something real will outperform thirty posts that say nothing.
Have an actual opinion: Great panel today, so much to think about is not an opinion. I disagreed with almost everything said in the third session, and here's why is an opinion.
Remember who's actually watching: The audience that matters on LinkedIn is very, very small. It's the handful of people in your field whose opinion of you has professional consequence.
